title: Mental Health: Understanding the Hidden Epidemic
paragraphs: Mental health is, in the words of the World Health Organisation, "a state of wellbeing in which an individual realises their own potential, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively, and is able to contribute to their community." By this definition, mental health is not merely the absence of mental illness — it is a positive state that enables people to live fully and function effectively. Yet despite growing public awareness, mental health remains one of the most neglected areas of global healthcare.

The scale of mental health conditions worldwide is striking. Approximately one in four people will experience a mental health condition at some point in their lives. Depression is the leading cause of disability globally, affecting over 280 million people. Anxiety disorders affect an estimated 284 million. These conditions impose enormous costs — not just on individuals and families, but on economies and healthcare systems. The World Economic Forum estimated that mental health conditions cost the global economy approximately $1 trillion per year in lost productivity.

Despite this scale, the global mental health treatment gap remains vast. In high-income countries, more than half of people with mental health conditions receive no treatment. In low- and middle-income countries, the figure rises to over 75%. The reasons are multiple: a shortage of trained mental health professionals, insufficient funding for mental health services, stigma that prevents people from seeking help, and healthcare systems that prioritise physical over psychological conditions. In many countries, the number of psychiatrists per 100,000 people is less than one.

Stigma — the social shame and discrimination associated with mental illness — is perhaps the most powerful barrier to treatment. Many people with depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia hide their conditions for fear of judgement from family, friends, employers, or society at large. They may lose jobs, relationships, or social standing if their condition becomes known. This stigma is not merely unkind — it is actively harmful, as it prevents people from seeking the help they need and delays recovery. Anti-stigma campaigns, celebrity disclosure, and education have made some progress in reducing stigma in certain communities, but much remains to be done.

The COVID-19 pandemic had a severe impact on global mental health. Social isolation, grief, economic uncertainty, and the disruption of normal routines contributed to a sharp increase in depression and anxiety, particularly among young people and healthcare workers. A 2021 WHO report found that the pandemic triggered a 25% increase in anxiety and depression globally. At the same time, the pandemic accelerated the adoption of digital mental health tools — apps, online therapy, and digital self-help resources — creating new possibilities for expanding access to support.

Effective treatments exist for most common mental health conditions. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a widely-used, evidence-based psychological treatment for depression and anxiety. Medication — antidepressants, mood stabilisers, antipsychotics — can be highly effective, particularly in combination with therapy. Exercise, sleep, social connection, and stress management are all well-evidenced lifestyle factors that support mental health. The challenge is not primarily scientific — it is about ensuring that these treatments are accessible, affordable, and free from stigma.

A genuinely healthy society takes mental health as seriously as physical health. This means investing in mental health services, training more professionals, integrating mental health into primary care, creating supportive workplaces and schools, and challenging the stigma that keeps people from getting help. Every person who suffers unnecessarily from an untreated mental health condition represents not just a personal tragedy, but a failure of the social systems that should be there to support them.
